solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Incarceration's a bit like a dessert topping, it's said

indicators.note: what is said is heard rather than read, so go by the pronunciation

parts.words: a bit like a dessert topping
parts.note: custard-y: rather like custard, the classic pudding topping

explanation.surface: Someone compares a prison stretch to a pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is a made-up adjective: something custardy is custard-like, and in a non-rhotic British accent it is pronounced just like custody.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: custody is the state of being held by the police or in prison.

clue.text: Lee's debut secured by having fresh set of Dracula teeth? Too modern

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so take the first letter

parts.words: having fresh set of Dracula teeth
parts.note: new-fanged: with new fangs, the teeth of a vampire like Dracula

indicators.note: something secured by another is held fast inside it

explanation.surface: Christopher Lee, the actor famous as Dracula, gets a fresh set of fangs for his first film.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Lee played Dracula in the Hammer horror films, which is what makes the surface hang together. NEWFANGED is not a real word; it is invented so the L can turn it into one.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: newfangled is the grumpy word for anything too new to be trusted.

clue.text: War's end included in settler's entreaty

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter
something included in another goes inside it

explanation.surface: A pioneer pleads for the fighting to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: A settler suggests a colonist, but here it is someone who settles an account.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an entreaty is an earnest plea, and a prayer is a plea made to a god.

clue.text: see 26dn.
Note: Rex has 'doo-dah' that's no longer tender

parts.note: the fourth note of the sol-fa scale
both are words for something you cannot name

explanation.surface: A king has an unnamed something that has become tough, or perhaps no longer sore.
explanation.walkthrough: Tender here means legal tender, money a shop must accept. A farthing was a quarter of an old British penny, withdrawn in 1961.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the old farthing coin was withdrawn in 1961 and stopped being legal tender.

clue.text: Trainer's small tool?

explanation.surface: A coach owns a little implement.
explanation.walkthrough: Trainer suggests a coach, but a trainer is also a sports shoe, the British word for a sneaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a trainer, the British name for a sneaker, is one kind of footwear.

clue.text: Sunak's beginning to be crushed by Right — boom!

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter
something crushed by another is squeezed in its middle

explanation.surface: Rishi Sunak is flattened by the right wing of his party with a bang.
explanation.walkthrough: Right looks like the political right, but it means correct, PROPER. Boom is a verb here, as in an economy booming.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both verbs: a booming business is one that thrives.

clue.text: Turn up a hunter's pants

indicators.note: British slang for rubbish, so the letters are a mess to be sorted

explanation.surface: A hunter's trousers are discovered.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants looks like underwear, but in British slang it also means rubbish, which signals rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to turn up a lost item is to dig it out, which is literally what unearthing does.

clue.text: Ambitious types of alien UFOs? Help!

indicators.note: the letters become strange and foreign, so rearrange them

explanation.surface: Someone cries for help at the sight of flying saucers.
explanation.walkthrough: Alien fits the UFO picture so well that it hides its job as the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: such people are aspiring to succeed, like would-be candidates in a contest.

clue.text: Kinky material puts energy into soap?

indicators.note: one part is placed somewhere
and that place is inside the other part

explanation.surface: Someone adds oomph to a steamy soap opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Soap suggests a TV soap opera, but it is the foam, LATHER.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this hide is the classic material of fetish clothing, hence kinky.

clue.text: Difficult part of golf course, said to be like pubic hair?

indicators.note: what is said is heard rather than read, so go by the pronunciation

parts.note: a tough tee: a hard spot to drive off from

explanation.surface: A golfer grumbles that the rough is as scratchy as a certain kind of hair.
explanation.walkthrough: The difficult part of a golf course looks like the rough, but it is a tough tee, the place each hole starts from.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: such hair grows in tufts.

clue.text: Futile instruction to cut the digital gesturing

parts.note: pointing with a digit, a finger
less! is an order to reduce

explanation.surface: A futile request to stop someone jabbing their finger.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an order: point less, meaning do less pointing. Digital means with the fingers, not electronic.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a futile effort has no purpose at all.

clue.text: Top level fallout when diamonds added to collar

explanation.surface: Nuclear fallout spreads at the top of government when jewels are pinned to a collar.
explanation.walkthrough: Top level fallout sounds like political or nuclear fallout, but it is flakes falling from the top of your head, often onto a collar.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the flakes of skin fall out from the top level of the body, the scalp.

clue.text: Morgan's endless, empty, cackle — prick!

indicators.note: a word without its end has lost its final letter

parts.note: Piers Morgan, the TV presenter: first name without its last letter

indicators.note: an empty word has had its contents removed, leaving only the outer letters

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at Piers Morgan for his endless, hollow cackling.
explanation.walkthrough: Morgan stands for his first name, Piers. Prick looks like an insult closing the rant, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both verbs: to prick a balloon is to puncture it.

clue.text: (& 24dn.) Group of supporters poisoned by Trump, turn appreciably sick

definitions.text: Group of supporters poisoned by Trump

indicators.note: the letters are unwell, disordered, and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Donald Trump's followers, having taken his poison, grow visibly ill.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across two grid entries: REPUBLICAN here and PARTY at 24 down. All fifteen letters of turn appreciably are used.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the US party whose supporters, the setter says, Trump has poisoned.

clue.text: Weight-watcher / a mouth opening = part of girth calculation

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A slimmer's equation for working out a waistline.
explanation.walkthrough: The slash marks where A and M go into DIETER; the clue gives no word for inserting, so the layout does the job.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: girth, a circumference, is calculated as pi times this width.

clue.text: Boris's duff economic policy, in bizarre leg-pull vein

indicators.note: the letters come out strange and need rearranging

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson's flagship policy is mocked as an odd practical joke.
explanation.walkthrough: A leg-pull is a practical joke, which is what the surface calls the policy.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: this was Boris Johnson's slogan for spreading prosperity to poorer British regions.

clue.text: Hugo sits on one at première of African Queen

indicators.note: in a down answer, a part that sits on another comes above it

explanation.surface: A novelist attends the opening night of the film The African Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The African Queen is a 1951 film, which glues the surface together; Queen alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the monarch who reigned over Britain from 1837 to 1901.

clue.text: A former Secretary of State pocketing duke's loan

indicators.note: one part slips another into its pocket

parts.note: A plus Cyrus Vance, US Secretary of State under Carter

explanation.surface: A retired statesman trousers a nobleman's loan.
explanation.walkthrough: Duke's reads as possessive, but the 's joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: money handed over before it is due, much like a loan.

clue.text: Caught in lie about government's top upper limit

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the word is read backwards
in a down answer the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A government is caught out lying about its spending cap.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are not in clue order: IN comes after the turned-round LIE in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: the top of a room, extended to any cap such as a price or debt limit.

clue.text: Balls trapped in Channel dock?

indicators.note: something trapped in another is caught inside it

parts.note: a channel for fluid or air
Ed Balls, the former Labour minister

explanation.surface: Footballs get stuck in a harbour on the English Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: Balls is a surname: Ed Balls is a British Labour politician turned TV personality. Dock is a verb, as in docking pay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both verbs: docking someone's pay means taking money off it.

clue.text: Cordial's a help to singers? Clever

explanation.surface: A fruit drink is praised as good for the voice.
explanation.walkthrough: Cordial looks like a soothing drink for the throat, but it is the adjective meaning friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: cordial relations are warm and friendly ones.

clue.text: Copper gets dude to isolate

parts.note: a toff is a posh, dandyish man

explanation.surface: A police officer gets a man to be kept apart.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper suggests a police officer, but it is the metal. A toff is British slang for an upper-class man.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both verbs: a village severed from the world by floods is isolated.

clue.text: see 15dn.
Playing truant, so a candidate for a rocket at rear?

definitions.text: candidate for a rocket at rear

indicators.note: the letters play around into a new order

explanation.surface: A pupil skipping school deserves a rocket up the backside.
explanation.walkthrough: A rocket is British slang for a severe telling-off. The definition turns this round: a space traveller rides a rocket firing at the rear.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a space traveller is a natural passenger for a rocket propelled from its rear.

clue.text: (& 4dn.) Ex-PM's only a bit useless, right?

indicators.note: letters in a useless state are wrecked and need putting back in order

explanation.surface: A sly aside that a former prime minister was only somewhat useless.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is split across two grid entries: TONY here and BLAIR at 4 down. The clue reads as a political jab, while useless is really the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Tony Blair led Labour and was British Prime Minister from 1997 to 2007.

clue.text: Fabric of time diminished royal

indicators.note: a diminished name is cut down to a shorter form

explanation.surface: A member of the royal family is worn down by the passing years.
explanation.walkthrough: Diminished here means reduced to a nickname: Will for William.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a woven cloth with diagonal ribs, used for denim and chinos.

clue.text: Can resident politician Vic start to testify?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A local asks whether a politician called Vic may begin giving evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: Can is not the verb but slang for prison, so a can resident is a prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang sense: the can is prison, and its resident is someone serving a sentence there.

clue.text: Forbear's infra-red balls died off

indicators.note: slang for nonsense, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: An ancestor's heat-seeking balls have dropped off.
explanation.walkthrough: Forbear looks like forebear, an ancestor, but it is the verb meaning hold back.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both verbs: to forbear from something is to hold back from doing it.
